title: The precepts of the Church (CCC 2041–2043)
hook: Sunday Mass, yearly confession, Easter communion, fasting, support

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace and merit: grace goes first, and even our merits are God's gifts. Your line was his gift in us. When someone thanked you, did you take it fully? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

Folding chairs, a box of donuts, a whiteboard with the marker running dry: a confirmation class in a church basement. A fifteen-year-old in the back raises his hand and asks a question others in the room may be wondering too: okay, but what's the least I have to do to still count? The catechist laughs, and then, instead of dodging, she writes a short list on the board. Five lines. Today's word is that list, and the surprising way the Church itself describes it.
screen: `A CHURCH BASEMENT, TUESDAY NIGHT.` → `WHAT'S THE LEAST I HAVE TO DO?` → `FIVE LINES ON A WHITEBOARD.`

segments.voice: The Catechism calls them the precepts of the Church, and it lists five. First: attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation, and rest from work that gets in the way of keeping the day holy. Second: confess your sins at least once a year. Third: receive Communion at least during the Easter season. Fourth: keep the days of fasting and abstinence the Church sets. Fifth: help provide for the needs of the Church, each according to their ability. That's the whole list. Short enough to fit on a whiteboard. Now the part that explains why that teenager deserved a straight answer. The Catechism doesn't present the precepts as the goal of the Christian life. It calls them a very necessary minimum: the least a Catholic owes in the spirit of prayer and moral effort, so that love of God and neighbor has room to grow. A floor, not a ceiling. Think of the list as the bones of a year. Every week, a Sunday. Every year, at least one confession and one Easter Communion. Certain days of fasting, when what the body wants is put second for a while. And the collection basket, or the time and skills given instead, so the parish lights stay on and the poor are fed. Each precept ties a Catholic's private life to the life of the whole Church, and the Catechism says these positive laws are meant to guarantee that minimum. So the honest answer to what's the least I have to do is this list. And the honest follow-up, which the Catechism makes, is that the least is only where it starts. Nobody falls in love and asks how few dinners they can get away with.
screen: `THE FIVE PRECEPTS.` · `SUNDAY, CONFESSION, EASTER, FASTING, SUPPORT.` · `A VERY NECESSARY MINIMUM.` · `A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check the five. Settle, and breathe. Go through the list slowly, one line at a time. Sunday. Confession. Easter Communion. Fasting days. Supporting the community. For each one, notice, without scolding yourself, where you are with it right now. If you're not Catholic, you can hold the list up to your own life and ask what your own small minimum is: the few things you keep no matter what. If you pray, you can ask for help with the one that's hardest. The bell holds the time.
Precepts. The five basic duties the Church asks of every Catholic: Sunday Mass, yearly confession, Easter Communion, fasting, and support for the Church. Today's word.
Your line: the minimum, not the maximum. Today, pick one of the five and do a little more than the least it asks. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught the five precepts in catechism classes; parishes post the holy days and the fasting days each year, and the precepts tie a Catholic's year to Sunday, Lent and Easter.
